lessons.title: School and studies
lessons.learn: Talk about classes, exams and homework using going-to future for near plans.

grammar.title: going to for plans
grammar.explain: Use be + going to + verb for a plan already decided.

examples.t: I'm going to revise tonight.
She's going to miss the lecture.
Are you going to finish the homework?

mistakes: Don't say 'I going to' — you need am/is/are.
Don't use going to for a spontaneous offer (use will).

dialogue.t: Have you got an exam tomorrow?
Yes, history. I'm going to revise after class.
Want to study together in the library?
Yes — the deadline for notes is tonight.

lessons.title: Hobbies and free time
lessons.learn: Say what you enjoy, how often, and suggest doing something together.

grammar.title: verb + -ing after enjoy/like
grammar.explain: After enjoy, like, mind, keep, use the -ing form.

examples.t: I enjoy playing guitar at weekends.
She doesn't mind waiting.
Keep practising if you want to join the team.

dialogue.t: What do you do at the weekend?
I play guitar. There's a concert on Saturday.
I enjoy sketching. Want to come?
Yes — after football practice.

lessons.title: Travel basics
lessons.learn: Buy tickets, ask for platforms, and handle a simple delay.

grammar.title: have to for necessity
grammar.explain: Have to expresses an external rule, not a personal wish.

examples.t: You have to show your passport at the gate.
We have to change at Leeds.
He doesn't have to book today.

mistakes: Don't confuse have to with must for rules you didn't choose.

dialogue.t: Single or return?
Return, please. Which platform?
Platform 4. There's a short delay.
Do I have to change?

lessons.title: Food and restaurants
lessons.learn: Order food, ask about ingredients, and send something back politely.

grammar.title: would like vs want
grammar.explain: Would like is the polite order form in restaurants.
grammar.pattern: I'd like + noun / I'd like to + verb

examples.t: I'd like the soup, please.
Would you like it spicy?
I'd like to see the menu.

mistakes: Want is fine with friends, blunt with waiters.

dialogue.t: Are you ready to order?
I'd like the pasta. Is it spicy?
A little. You're not allergic?
No. The bill at the end, please.

lessons.title: Friends and social life
lessons.learn: Make, accept and refuse invitations without sounding rude.

grammar.title: Shall we / Why don't we
grammar.explain: These two frames make a suggestion, not an order.
grammar.pattern: Shall we + verb? / Why don't we + verb?

examples.t: Shall we meet at seven?
Why don't we catch up next week?
Let's bring some food.

mistakes: Shall we is a question, not 'shall I you'.
Don't refuse with only 'no' — give a reason.

dialogue.t: There's a party on Friday. Shall we go?
I'm busy Friday. Why don't we catch up next week?
Sunday? I'm free after six.
Perfect. I'll bring dessert.

lessons.title: Weather and plans
lessons.learn: Describe weather and change a plan because of it.

grammar.title: first conditional
grammar.explain: If + present, will + verb: a real future possibility.

examples.t: If it rains, we'll cancel the picnic.
If the forecast is clear, we'll walk.
If it doesn't clear up, we'll stay indoor.

mistakes: Don't use will in the if-clause.

dialogue.t: The forecast says showers.
If it rains, we'll go to the museum.
Take an umbrella anyway.
If it clears up, we'll walk by the river.

lessons.title: Shopping and money
lessons.learn: Compare prices, ask for sizes, and talk about refunds.

grammar.title: comparatives
grammar.explain: Add -er to short adjectives; use more with long ones.

examples.t: This shirt is cheaper than that one.
The blue one is more expensive.
It fits better in size M.

mistakes: Don't forget than in a comparison.

dialogue.t: Are you paying by card or cash?
Card. Have you got this in a smaller size?
Yes. Keep the receipt for a refund.
Is there a student discount?

lessons.title: Daily routines and future plans
lessons.learn: Describe a weekday and a plan for next month without mixing tenses.

grammar.title: present simple vs going to
grammar.explain: Present simple is the timetable; going to is your decision.
grammar.pattern: I usually + verb  /  I'm going to + verb

examples.t: I usually commute at seven.
I'm going to save next month.
My shift starts at nine.

mistakes: Don't use present continuous for a permanent habit.
Don't use going to for a printed timetable.

dialogue.t: What time do you usually start?
My shift starts at nine. I'm going to change it next month.
Why?
I want a shorter commute. That's the goal.
